__Situation (again):__ Suppose that you are interested in purchasing a used car. How much should you expect to pay?  Obviously the price will depend on the type of car you get (the model) and how much it's been used. For this assignment you will investigate how the price might depend on the age, mileage, and the model of car. 

__Data Source:__ To get a sample of vehicles, begin with the _vehiclesSE_ csv file. The data was acquired by scraping Craigslist for vehicles for sale across the southeastern United States. For this assignment, you will need to select six new samples, each with _exactly_ 50 vehicles, for six different _model_ of used vehicles for sale on Craigslist in the Southeastern United States. There will likely be more than 50 of your selected models for sale in the _vehiclesSE_ datset, so you should randomly select those 50 vehicles from the larger number that are available (and are listed with a _price_ greater than $0). The six models of vehicles should be selected such that three models of vehicles are selected from Japanese companies, and another three from US companies (i.e. _manufacturer_; It does not matter where the cars were actually made). Within each country, you should select a compact car, a mid-sized car, and a SUV (Note that the country and types of vehicles are not given in the data and are for you to determine). You should add new variables to the dataframes for the country of the company and type of vehicle (compact vs mid-sized vs SUV) and combine these six samples into one dataframe (use rbind(df1, df2, df3, ...)). When selecting these samples make sure to use set.seed(). This will select the same sample each time that you run (and knit) your code.The code below is an example of how you could select a random sample of 50 cars for a given model:

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

vehiclesSE <- read_csv("/Users/jimmyzheng0516/Desktop/STOR455/vehiclesSE.csv", show_col_types = F)

set.seed(8675309) # VERY IMPORTANT!
Japan_1 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="civic" & price > 0), 50) # Compact
Japan_2 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="camry" & price > 0), 50) # mid-size
Japan_3 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="rav4" & price > 0), 50) # SUV
US_1 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="cruze" & price > 0), 50) # Compact
US_2 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="enclave" & price > 0), 50) # mid-size
US_3 = sample_n(subset(vehiclesSE, model=="wrangler" & price > 0), 50) # SUV

df_reg = as.data.frame(rbind(Japan_1, Japan_2, Japan_3, US_1, US_2, US_3))

df_reg$country = as.factor(ifelse(df_reg$model == "civic"|df_reg$model == "camry"|df_reg$model == "rav4", "Japan", "US"))
df_reg$type = as.factor(ifelse(df_reg$model == "civic"|df_reg$model == "cruze", "compact", 
                               ifelse(df_reg$model == "camry"|df_reg$model == "enclave", "mid-size", 
                                      ifelse(df_reg$model == "rav4"|df_reg$model == "wrangler", "SUV", ""))))
```

#### One Way ANOVA ####    

1.  Produce a set of side-by-side boxplots to compare the price distributions of your three types of vehicles (not the models). Comment on any obvious differences in the distributions. 

```{r}
boxplot(price~type, data = df_reg)
```
As the car type changes from compact to mid-size and SUV, car prices tend to be higher given the increasing median and IQRs. The spread of prices also tends to be larger as the car type changes from compact to mid-size and SUV; SUV and mid-size cars' IQRs and Ranges are larger than that of compact cars. 

2.  Produce summary statistics (mean and standard deviation) for each of the groups (vehicle types) AND the entire sample of vehicle prices. 

```{r}
# Summary Statistics by Groups
tapply(df_reg$price, df_reg$type, mean)
tapply(df_reg$price, df_reg$type, sd)

# Summary Statistics of the entire sample of vehicle prices
mean(df_reg$price)
sd(df_reg$price)
```

3.  Based on just what you see in the boxplots and summary statistics comment on whether you think there are significant differences in the mean prices among your three vehicle types. Also comment on any concerns you see about the conditions for the ANOVA for means model.

Compared to the mean vehicle price of the entire sample, mean prices by car types differ significantly; noticeably, SUV mean price is as twice as compact's mean price, while midsize have mean prices similar to the overall mean price.

Concerns about the ANOVA conditions:
The standard deviations of prices for different car types differ a lot: compact's standard deviations is about the half of mid-size and SUV's. This signifies that constant variance condition is also unlikely to be met. Based on the existing information, whether normality of residuals is met is still unknown.

4.  Construct an ANOVA model for the mean price by vehicle type. Include the output showing the ANOVA table; state hypotheses, and provide a conclusion in the context of your data. 

```{r}
mod1 = aov(price~type, data = df_reg)
summary(mod1)
```
H0: mean car prices from different car types are the same
Ha: at least one of the car types produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is 1.78e-15 < 0.01, so we conclude that car type does make a difference in mean car prices at any conventional significance level.

5.  Produce plots and/or summary statistics to comment on the appropriateness of the following conditions for your data: normality of the residuals, and equality of the variances. If you find that the conditions are _not_ met, You can still continue with analysis of your data for this homework. We will soon discuss how to deal with violations of these conditions.

```{r}
plot(mod1, 1:2)
```

Based on the qq-norm plot of the residuals, it seems that normality condition is not perfectly met as the two tails deviate significantly from the qq-norm line. There is also concerns about the constant variance condition; as shown in the residual-fitted plot, the spread of residuals tend to increase as fitted value increases.

6.  If your ANOVA model indicates that there are significant differences among the vehicle type price means, discuss where the significant differences occur using Tukey HSD methods. If your ANOVA indicates there are not significant differences among the vehicle type price means, determine how different your mean prices would need to be in order to find a significant difference using the Tukey HSD methods.

```{r}
TukeyHSD(mod1)
```
From the Tukey's confidence intervals, we observe that the differences in mean prices are basically significant among every pair of car types. SUV-compact and SUV-mid-size are the most significant pairs with p-values near zero.


#### Two Way ANOVA ####

7.  Construct an ANOVA model for the mean price using the country of the company and the type of vehicle as predictors (without an interaction). Include the output showing the ANOVA table; state hypotheses and provide a conclusion in the context of your data. If your ANOVA model indicates there are significant differences among the vehicle price means: Discuss where the significant differences occur using Tukey HSD methods.

```{r}
mod2 = aov(price~country+type, data = df_reg)
summary(mod2)
```
Hypothesis for "country"
H0: mean car prices from different countries are the same
Ha: at least one of the car manufacturer's country produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is 4.57e-05 < 0.01, so we conclude that manufacturer's country does make a difference in mean car prices at any conventional significance level.

Hypothesis for "type"
H0: mean car prices from different car types are the same
Ha: at least one of the car types produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is 3.51e-16 < 0.01, so we conclude that car type does make a difference in mean car prices at any conventional significance level.

```{r}
TukeyHSD(mod2)
```
Based on the Tukey comparisons, the differences come from both country and all most every pair of car types as they all produced extremely significant p-values less then 0.01. Nevertheless, mid-size-compact seems to have slightly higher p-value of 0.0129982, but it is still significant at 5% confidence interval.

8.	Produce plots and/or summary statistics to comment on the appropriateness of the following conditions for your data: normality of the residuals, and equality of the variances. 

```{r}
plot(mod2, 1:2)
```
Based on the residual plots, normality is not perfectly met as residuals at the right tails deviate significantly from the qq-norm line. Constant variance is mostly met except for some small fitted values (price lower than 8,000 & price around 10,000) with smaller spreads of residuals than the others. 

9.  Construct an ANOVA model for the mean price using the country of the company and the type of vehicle as predictors with the interaction. Include the output showing the ANOVA table; state hypotheses and provide a conclusion in the context of your data. If your ANOVA indicates that there are significant differences among the car price means: Discuss where the significant differences occur using Tukey HSD methods.

```{r}
mod3 = aov(price~country+type+country*type, data = df_reg)
summary(mod3)
```
Hypothesis for "country"
H0: mean car prices from different countries are the same
Ha: at least one of the car manufacturer's country produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is 3.91e-05 < 0.01, so we conclude that manufacturer's country does make a difference in mean car prices at any conventional significance level.

Hypothesis for "type"
H0: mean car prices from different car types are the same
Ha: at least one of the car types produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is < 2e-16 < 0.01, so we conclude that car type does make a difference in mean car prices at any conventional significance level.

Hypothesis for the interaction between "country and "type":

H0: mean car prices from interactions between "country" and "type" are the same
Ha: at least one of the above interaction produces different mean price from the others' means

The p-value of the F-statistic is 0.0254 < 0.05, so we conclude that the interaction effect does make a difference in mean car prices at 5% significance level.

10. Produce two interaction plots for the previous model. If you found significant interactions in your hypothesis test, comment on how these interactions are shown in the plot. If you did not find significant interactions in your hypothesis test, comment on how the (lack of) interactions are shown in the plot.

```{r}
interaction.plot(df_reg$country, df_reg$type, df_reg$price)
```
As car manufacturer's country shifts from Japan to the US, mean car price rises most substantially for SUV and least substantially for compact cars. This signifies that car type has an interaction effect on mean car price when car manufacturer's country varies. 

```{r}
interaction.plot(df_reg$type, df_reg$country, df_reg$price)
```
As car type shifts from compact to mid-size and SUV, the change in mean price of American cars is larger than that of Japanese cars. This signifies that car manufacturer's country has an interaction effect on mean car price when car type varies.

#### Additional Topics ####
11. Recall that we can also handle a categorical predictor with multiple categories using ordinary multiple regression if we create indicator variables for each category and include all but one of the indicators in the model. Run an ordinary multiple regression to predict _price_ using the country of the company, the type of vehicle, and the interaction between the two as predictors. Interpret each of the coefficients in the "dummy" regression by what they mean in the context of mean prices. 

```{r}
mod_lm = lm(price~country+type+country*type, data = df_reg)
summary(mod_lm)
```
Interpretation of Slope Estimates:
Slope Estimate (Intercept) = the mean price of a Japanese compact car is $8006.7.
Slope Estimate countryUS = the difference between the mean price of a US compact car and that of a Japanese compact car is $478.2.
Slope Estimate typemid-size = the difference between the mean price of a Japanese mid-size car and that of a Japanese compact car is $1178.4.
Slope Estimate typeSUV  = the difference between the mean price of a Japanese SUV and that of a Japanese compact car is $6247.1.
Slope Estimate countryUS:typemid-size = the difference between the mean price of a US mid-size car and that of a Japanese compact car is $3460.0.
Slope Estimate countryUS:typeSUV = the difference between the mean price of a US SUV and that of a Japanese compact car is $5453.8.

12. One possible drawback of the analysis for this assignment is that different people might have chosen vehicles with quite different mileages when collecting their samples.  Thus an apparent "difference" between two countries or vehicle types might be due to one sample having considerably more higher mileage vehicles in it than another. Construct a model that allows you to check for mean price differences between your vehicles from the model constructed in question 11 after accounting for variability due to the _odometer_ readings of the vehicles. Explain how you use the output from the model to address this question.

```{r}
mod4 = lm(price~odometer+country+type, data = df_reg)
anova(mod4)
```

Based on the ANOVA output, the covariate odometer, factor country, and factor type are all significant in explaining the variability of the car prices as they all have p-value < 0.01. Even though odometer is included in the model, car manufacturer's country and car type still account for significant amount of variability in the car prices as they did in previous models. 

Exploring the need of including interaction terms between odometer and those dummy factors:

```{r}
country1 = subset(df_reg, country=="US")
country2 = subset(df_reg, country=="Japan")

lm.US = lm(price~odometer, data = country1)
lm.Japan = lm(price~odometer, data = country2)

plot(price~odometer, data = df_reg)
abline(lm.US, col="red")
abline(lm.Japan, col="blue")
legend(220000, 40000, legend=c("US", "Japan"),
       col=c("red", "blue"), lty=1, cex=0.8)
```
Based on the plot above, it seems that including an interaction term between odometer and country is unnecessary as their regression lines are roughly parallel: for an mile increase in odometer, car prices decrease by roughly the same amount for a US car compared with a Japanese car.

```{r}
type1 = subset(df_reg, type=="compact")
type2 = subset(df_reg, type=="mid-size")
type3 = subset(df_reg, type=="SUV")

lm.compact = lm(price~odometer, data = type1)
lm.midsize = lm(price~odometer, data = type2)
lm.SUV = lm(price~odometer, data = type3)

plot(price~odometer, data = df_reg)
abline(lm.compact, col="red")
abline(lm.midsize, col="blue")
abline(lm.SUV, col="green")
legend(200000, 40000, legend=c("compact", "mid-size", "SUV"),
       col=c("red", "blue", "green"), lty=1, cex=0.8)
```
Based on the plot above, it seems that including an interaction term between odometer and type is necessary as the regression line for compact cars differ from the lines of mid-size cars and SUV: for an mile increase in odometer, car prices decrease by a smaller amount for a compact car compared with a mid-size car or a SUV.
